args.body:
MEMORANDUM

TO: File
FROM: Arbitration & International Dispute Resolution Practice Group
RE: Counterparty Markup Analysis — Arbitration Agreement (Accept/Reject/Counter Memorandum)
DATE: [DATE]

_______________________________________________________________________________

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have completed a full review of the counterparty's redline of the arbitration agreement against (i) our original draft and firm-standard provisions, (ii) the operative SPA excerpts and disclosure schedules, and (iii) the internal negotiating position and firm guidance. The counterparty's markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations that warrant careful scrutiny:

1.  A silent reduction of the indemnification cap and conversion of the indemnity basket from a deductible structure to a tipping-basket structure.
2.  Expansion of the Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") definition to carve out regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this transaction.
3.  Introduction of a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations.

Of these three deviations, the deal team's controlling instruction (as confirmed in the most recent partner correspondence) is that the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any reduction in the survival period as a walk-away issue. This memorandum analyzes each deviation in detail, reconciles the markup against the disclosure schedules (particularly Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B), and sets out our recommended accept/reject/counter positions.

_______________________________________________________________________________

II. BACKGROUND AND CONTROLLING INSTRUCTIONS

A. Engagement Scope

This matter concerns the proposed arbitration agreement negotiated between the parties in connection with the underlying transaction. The operative agreement contains representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions negotiated between the parties. The counterparty's latest markup introduces deviations from the firm-standard provisions that must be evaluated against the base agreement, the SPA disclosure schedules, and internal negotiation guidance.

B. Controlling Policy Instruction

The most recent partner email thread on this engagement REVISES the analysis priorities for this matter. The latest message, which controls over all earlier messages, establishes the following:

• The client will concede the basket conversion (i.e., the conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket is acceptable). This is a settled concession and should not be treated as a point of contention in the deliverable.

• Any reduction in the survival period for the core representations is treated as a walk-away issue. This is a non-negotiable point. If the counterparty insists on shortening survival, the client is prepared to walk away from the deal rather than accept the shortened period.

Earlier messages in the thread stated the opposite priority ordering (i.e., that survival-period reduction was concedable and the basket conversion was a priority concern). Those earlier instructions are superseded and must not be followed.

The deliverable must reflect the controlling instruction.

C. Sources Considered

In preparing this memorandum, we reviewed the following source materials:

1. Original agreed draft of the arbitration agreement and firm-standard provisions;
2. Counterparty's markup introducing the deviations analyzed herein;
3. SPA excerpts and disclosure schedules, including:
   - Schedule 3.7 (disclosing two pending regulatory inquiries);
   - Schedule 5.2 (listing retained liabilities);
   - Exhibit B (setting the survival matrix for representations and warranties);
4. Internal negotiation playbook and firm guidance on standard positions, approved fallbacks, and escalation triggers.

_______________________________________________________________________________

III. DEVIATION 1: INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET REVERSAL

A. Counterparty's Markup

The counterparty's revision does two things to the indemnification provisions:

(i) It silently reduces the indemnification cap from the firm-standard level agreed in the base draft to a lower figure; and

(ii) It converts the indemnity basket from a deductible structure to a tipping-basket structure.

Under a deductible structure, the indemnifying party is responsible only for losses exceeding the basket threshold. Under a tipping-basket structure, once the threshold is met, the indemnifying party becomes liable for the entire amount of losses from the first dollar (i.e., the basket "tips" and the cap applies to all losses, including those below the threshold). The change from a deductible to a tipping basket shifts risk materially in favor of the counterparty by making them liable for the full amount of covered losses once the basket is satisfied.

Additionally, the cap reduction compounds the risk-inversion: even if the tipping basket is deemed acceptable per the client's concession, the reduced cap directly diminishes the client's recovery exposure in the event of a breach.

B. Reconciliation with Schedule 5.2

Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. These retained liabilities were previously the counterparty's responsibility and were not subject to the indemnification cap or basket. Under the markup's revised cap and basket mechanics, these liabilities could become subject to, and thereby limited by, the reduced cap and the new basket structure. This is a hidden course shift that effectively transfers previously uncapped, first-dollar liability exposure into the capped, basket-gated indemnification framework.

We note that the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Because Schedule 5.2 enumerates specific retained liabilities, any modification to the indemnification framework that would capture those liabilities must be resisted unless expressly agreed by the parties.

C. Analysis

The basket conversion, while it does shift risk toward the counterparty (favoring the client), has been conceded by the client per the controlling partner instruction. We therefore do not recommend treating the basket reversal as a negotiation point.

However, the silent reduction of the indemnification cap is a separate and distinct deviation that has NOT been conceded. This reduction:
- Alters the economic allocation of risk agreed in the base draft;
- Reduces the client's aggregate recovery for breaches of representations, warranties, and covenants;
- Interacts with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities to further reduce the client's protection; and
- Was not flagged or justified by the counterparty in negotiation correspondence.

The cap reduction should be rejected, and we should counter at the firm-standard cap level agreed in the base draft.

D. Recommendation: REJECT the cap reduction; CONCEDE the basket conversion.

• Reject the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. Counter at the firm-standard cap from the base draft.
• Concede the deductible-to-tipping basket conversion per the controlling partner instruction. No further negotiation required on this point.
• Ensure that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities remain outside the cap and basket framework. If the counterparty resists, escalate for further guidance.

_______________________________________________________________________________

IV. DEVIATION 2: MAE CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION

A. Counterparty's Markup

The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." In substance, the proposed carve-out would exclude from the MAE definition any adverse effect caused by, or arising from, regulatory inquiries, investigations, or actions of the type disclosed or contemplated in this matter.

B. Reconciliation with Schedule 3.7

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect precisely with the MAE carve-outs the counterparty has introduced. In other words, the counterparty is seeking to add an MAE carve-out for regulatory action that will cover precisely the two pending regulatory inquiries already disclosed on Schedule 3.7.

The practical effect is significant: if the MAE definition is amended to carve out regulatory action of the kind disclosed on Schedule 3.7, then the two pending regulatory inquiries would not constitute (or contribute to the determination of) a Material Adverse Effect. This would deprive the client of a potential MAE-based termination right or condition-to-closing basis if those pending inquiries materially worsen or lead to adverse outcomes.

Because the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, and because Schedule 3.7 specifically discloses these two inquiries, the counterparty's carve-out would operate to nullify the very disclosures the counterparty was required to make. That is, the counterparty would be able to say: (i) we disclosed the pending regulatory inquiries (satisfying our disclosure obligation), and (ii) those same disclosed regulatory inquiries are carved out from the MAE definition (eliminating the client's recourse based on them).

C. Analysis

This deviation is particularly concerning for several reasons:

1. It is designed to eliminate the client's ability to rely on MAE conditions related to the specific regulatory exposure already identified in this matter.

2. It operates asymmetrically: while the counterparty benefits from the carve-out, the client has no corresponding protection or alternative recourse.

3. It undermines the purpose of Schedule 3.7 disclosure. The disclosures were made to place the client on notice of the regulatory inquiries; carving those same inquiries out of the MAE definition effectively converts the disclosure from a protective mechanism for the client into a mechanism for insulating the counterparty.

4. It is drafted in a way that is overbroad — the carve-out applies to regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue" rather than being narrowly scoped to specific, enumerated matters.

D. Recommendation: REJECT the MAE carve-out in its entirety.

The counterparty's proposed MAE carve-out for regulatory action is unacceptable in its present form. We recommend:

• Rejecting the carve-out in its entirety.
• If the counterparty insists on addressing regulatory exposure in the MAE definition, counter with a narrowly scoped provision that (i) does not reference the two Schedule 3.7 inquiries, (ii) applies only to regulatory actions that were publicly known and disclosed prior to signing, and (iii) requires that any MAE determination take into account the ongoing regulatory inquiries on a forward-looking basis, including any material escalation.
• Do not concede the carve-out without further guidance from the deal team and confirmation from special counsel on regulatory exposure.

_______________________________________________________________________________

V. DEVIATION 3: NEW LIMITATION PERIOD SHORTENING SURVIVAL FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

A. Counterparty's Markup

The counterparty introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations. Under the base agreement and Exhibit B to the SPA, the survival matrix sets specific survival periods for the representations and warranties, with the core/fundamental representations surviving longer (often for the applicable statute of limitations or a negotiated multi-year period) than non-core representations.

The counterparty's markup proposes to shorten the survival period for these core representations — a change that contradicts Exhibit B.

B. Reconciliation with Exhibit B

Exhibit B to the SPA sets the survival matrix for representations and warranties in this matter. The survival matrix establishes, among other things, the period during which the indemnified party may bring claims for breaches of the representations. The counterparty's proposed limitation-period change directly contradicts the survival periods set forth in Exhibit B.

Because the scheduled exceptions and exhibits control over general statements in the base materials, Exhibit B's survival matrix is the operative reference point. The counterparty's markup seeks to undermine that operative schedule.

C. Analysis

The survival-period reduction is the most consequential deviation in the counterparty's markup. Under the controlling partner instruction, any reduction in the survival period for core representations is a walk-away issue. The rationale is straightforward: the survival period defines the client's window to discover and pursue claims for breaches of the fundamental representations. Shortening that window materially diminishes the value of the representations and the client's ability to hold the counterparty accountable.

The counterparty's proposed change also operates in tension with the Schedule 3.7 inquiry disclosures. Pending regulatory inquiries frequently remain unresolved for extended periods. A shortened survival period could cause the survival window to expire before the outcome of those inquiries is finally determined, potentially leaving the client without recourse for losses that crystallize after the survival period lapses.

D. Recommendation: REJECT — WALK-AWAY ISSUE.

Per the controlling partner instruction, any reduction in the survival period for the core representations is a non-negotiable, walk-away issue. We recommend:

• Rejecting the limitation-period change in its entirety.
• Restoring the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B without modification.
• Communicating to the counterparty that a shortened survival period for core representations is a fundamental deal term and will not be accepted.
• If the counterparty refuses to withdraw the limitation-period change, escalate immediately to the partner and the client for a go/no-go determination, given the client's position that survival-period reduction is a walk-away matter.
• Do not offer a counterproposal with a shortened survival period under any circumstances on the core representations (including the fundamental representations and the Schedule 3.7-related disclosures).

_______________________________________________________________________________

VI. ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

A. Reconciliation of Multiple Deviations

The three deviations do not operate in isolation. Their combined effect is more adverse to the client than any single deviation alone:

• The MAE carve-out (Deviation 2) limits the client's ability to terminate or withhold closing based on regulatory deterioration;
• The survival-period reduction (Deviation 3) shortens the client's window to pursue claims after closing; and
• The cap reduction (Deviation 1) further limits the client's aggregate recovery.

Taken together, these changes would leave the client with a substantially reduced set of rights: no MAE-based exit for the specific regulatory exposure, a shorter claims window, and a lower aggregate cap. This combination underscores the importance of treating the deviations independently and resisting the "package deal" framing the counterparty may advance.

B. The Distractor Document

Administrative correspondence misfiled into the matter folder (labeled "Unrelated correspondence — administrative file 2") concerns a different client engagement and must be disregarded. It provides no basis for any position taken in this analysis.

C. Scheduling Considerations

The disclosure schedules qualify the base materials. Each scheduled exception narrows a representation the counterparty markup also touches. In every instance where a scheduled exception intersects with a markup deviation, the scheduled exception controls. This principle has been applied consistently throughout this analysis.

_______________________________________________________________________________

VII. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

| Deviation | Counterparty Proposal | Recommendation | Rationale |
|-----------|----------------------|----------------|-----------|
| 1a. Indemnification cap | Silent reduction of the cap | REJECT — counter at firm-standard cap | Not conceded by client; silently shifts risk; interacts adversely with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities |
| 1b. Basket structure | Deductible → tipping basket | CONCEDE | Client concession per controlling partner instruction |
| 2. MAE carve-outs | Carve-outs for regulatory action of kind at issue | REJECT in its entirety | Directly undermines Schedule 3.7 disclosures; overbroad; asymmetric risk allocation |
| 3. Survival period | New shortened limitation period | REJECT — WALK-AWAY ISSUE | Contradicts Exhibit B survival matrix; core reps survival is non-negotiable per partner instruction; client will walk away |

_______________________________________________________________________________

VIII. NEXT STEPS

1. Prepare and send a counter-redline to the counterparty, incorporating the following positions:
   - Reject the indemnification cap reduction; counter at the firm-standard cap;
   - Accept the basket conversion (deductible → tipping);
   - Reject the MAE carve-out in its entirety, with no suggestion of a compromise unless further instructed;
   - Reject the survival-period limitation change and restore Exhibit B survival matrix without modification.

2. Flag to the partner and deal team that the MAE carve-out (Deviation 2) and the survival-period reduction (Deviation 3) each independently constitute material deviations that, if not withdrawn, may warrant escalation.

3. Prepare a separate escalation memorandum quantifying the aggregate financial impact of the three deviations, including the interaction with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities and the Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries, as required by the internal playbook for any term that exceeds approved fallback thresholds.

4. Schedule a review session with the deal team to confirm the counter-redline positions prior to delivery, particularly if any counterparty resistance is anticipated on the MAE carve-out.

_______________________________________________________________________________

Prepared by: Arbitration & International Dispute Resolution Practice Group
Matter: Arbitration International Dispute Resolution — Counterparty Markup Analysis
